ghurba.label: Living abroad and homesickness
ghurba.insight: Living far from home is not, in the Prophetic way, a weakness of faith or a betrayal of one's homeland and family: the Quran mentions the Prophet ﷺ leaving his own city “when those who disbelieved had driven him out”, and it mentions Musa (peace be upon him) arriving in Madyan as a lone stranger and turning to his Lord: “My Lord, indeed I am, for whatever good You would send down to me, in need.” Longing for family and homeland is a natural feeling no one is blamed for; what matters is that it turns into keeping ties, kindness and prayer, not into withdrawing from the present. Out of Allah's mercy, “when a servant falls ill or travels, the like of what he used to do when at home and in good health is recorded for him”; what a move keeps you from doing is not lost if your intention is sincere. So build where you are: ties with your family, good company, an identity you are proud of without closing yourself off, and getting to know people, as Allah says: “and made you peoples and tribes that you may know one another.”

now: Call your family today, a short call for no particular reason; keeping ties needs no occasion
Name exactly what you miss: people? language? food? the atmosphere of worship? A specific longing is easier to deal with
Pray with the words of Musa when he was a stranger: “My Lord, indeed I am, for whatever good You would send down to me, in need”
week: Look for a nearby mosque, Islamic centre or community, and attend at least one gathering
List your pending official procedures and their deadlines, and ask the official body or a trusted legal-aid organisation about them, not rumour groups
Get to know a neighbour or colleague from your new country; getting to know one another is a Quranic aim and a path to feeling at home
long: Give keeping in touch with your family a fixed time, such as a weekly call, instead of waiting for a free moment
Teach your children your language and your family's stories with love, not pressure, and let them be proud of where they belong without conflict
Every now and then ask yourself: why did I come? Does that reason still hold? A conscious decision weighs less than a vague longing

questions: What do you really miss: the people, the place, or a version of yourself that lived there?
What have you built here that deserves your gratitude to Allah despite the hard beginning?
Are you living your present, or postponing it until an undecided day of return?
avoid: Cutting yourself off completely from your new society, or dissolving into it until you lose your faith and identity
Relying on rumours for official procedures instead of official sources and specialists
Punishing yourself for being far from your family; being away for a legitimate reason while keeping ties and kindness does not mean you have failed them
ghurba.help: For residence, asylum, contracts and rights, seek help from an official body, a lawyer or a trusted legal-aid organisation, and do not rely on advice from unverified groups.

transition.label: Change and adjusting
transition.insight: Change is one of the patterns of life, and the Quran teaches us not to judge beginnings by our first feelings: “But perhaps you hate a thing and it is good for you.” The Hijra itself was a move and a new beginning, prepared for with means and planning together with complete reliance on Allah, and the Prophet ﷺ taught us to combine the two: “Tie it and rely upon Allah.” The way to handle beginnings is to accept the first phase of confusion without judging the whole road by it, to start with something small and steady, for “the deeds most beloved to Allah are those done most consistently, even if they are few”, and to ask Allah for right guidance: “Our Lord, grant us from Yourself mercy and prepare for us from our affair right guidance.”

now: Write down three things that have changed and three that have stayed the same: your faith, your values, and those who love you
Choose one small, steady routine to keep in this new phase: a prayer on time, a walk, or a short daily remembrance
Pray: “Our Lord, grant us from Yourself mercy and prepare for us from our affair right guidance”
week: Get to know one person in the new place, and ask what a newcomer most needs
Break adjusting into small tasks (papers, routes, places, people) and finish one each day
Give yourself a reasonable time to adjust before you judge the decision a failure
long: After three months, review: what have I learned? What needs adjusting?
Build meaning for this phase: what good can you offer here that was not possible before?
Keep in touch with those who were with you in the previous phase; change does not mean cutting ties

questions: Are you judging the new phase by its first confusing days?
What do you carry from the previous phase that deserves to continue?
What is the smallest step that would make this place or this role feel more like yours?
avoid: Comparing a new beginning with the end of a previous phase you had years to settle into
Turning back hastily at the first difficulty before the experience has had its time
Neglecting worship and rest because you are busy with arrangements

emergency.label: Emergencies and sudden setbacks
emergency.insight: Unpleasant surprises are part of the nature of this world, and the Prophetic way teaches three things when they happen: steadiness in the first moment, for “patience is only at the first strike (of a calamity)”; letting go of self-blame through “if only”: “If something befalls you, do not say: ‘If only I had done such and such, it would have been so and so,’ but say: ‘Allah has decreed, and what He wills He does’”; and then moving straight to action: “Strive for what benefits you, seek help from Allah, and do not give up.” It also teaches taking precautions before an emergency happens, “Tie it and rely upon Allah”, such as keeping copies of documents and leaving some margin of time and money. Whoever is struck should ask for help without embarrassment, and whoever sees someone in distress should help them, for “he who relieves a believer of one of the hardships of this world, Allah will relieve him of one of the hardships of the Day of Resurrection.”

now: Stop and breathe, and say: “Allah has decreed, and what He wills He does”
Set the priority: your safety and the safety of those with you first, then whatever can be saved now
If there is danger or injury, call emergency services immediately, and do not hesitate to ask the people around you for help
week: Complete the procedures step by step: an official report, replacing documents, contacting the bank or the relevant office
Write down what the situation taught you, without blame: what precaution would prevent it happening again?
Thank whoever helped you, even with a word; “He who does not thank the people is not thankful to Allah”
long: Keep digital copies of your important documents, and a small sum for emergencies
Learn basic first aid; you may save a life with it
Be the help others need in their emergencies

questions: Can what happened be fixed, or does it need to be accepted? What is the next step in either case?
Are you blaming yourself with “if only” more than you are looking for a solution?
Who can you ask for help right now?
avoid: Hasty decisions under the shock of the moment
Blaming yourself or others instead of focusing on the solution
Being too embarrassed to ask for help when you need it
emergency.help: If there is danger to life, an injury or a fire, call your country's emergency number immediately, before anything else.

digital.label: Online life and privacy
digital.insight: The digital world is part of our lives, and the values of the Quran and Sunnah govern it just as they govern real life: every written word is recorded, “Man does not utter any word except that with him is an observer prepared [to record]”; news that is circulating must be checked before it is shared, “if there comes to you a disobedient one with information, investigate”; people's privacy is protected, “and do not spy”; and a single word can raise a person or bring them down. It is wise to be wary of suspicious links and messages, “Leave what makes you doubt for what does not make you doubt”, and “a believer is not stung twice from one and the same hole.” Time is a blessing many neglect: “There are two blessings in which many people are deceived: health and free time.” If you are threatened or blackmailed, do not give in and do not face it alone: keep the evidence and ask for help; the sin of harm lies with the one who causes it.

now: Do not reply to the blackmailer or the person threatening you, do not send money or photos, and keep screenshots as evidence
Change your password immediately, and turn on two-step verification if your account is at risk
Before sharing or forwarding news, ask: have I checked it? Would I be happy for it to be attributed to me?
week: Review the privacy settings of your accounts: who sees your posts, your photos and your numbers?
Delete or archive what no longer represents you, without fear or self-punishment
Set phone-free times: at bedtime, with your family, and during prayer
long: Give every post one question: would I be pleased to see this in my record of deeds?
Gently teach your children and the elderly in your family the basics of online safety
Make your worth independent of likes and followers; Allah “does not look to your faces and your wealth, but He looks to your hearts and to your deeds”

questions: If the people you respect read what you write, would you change any of it?
Are you using your phone, or is it using you? How much of your time goes without you choosing it?
Have you checked the news before carrying the burden of spreading it?
avoid: Giving in to blackmail or paying money; this usually increases the demands rather than stopping them
Sharing passwords or private photos with anyone, even out of trust
Spreading news before verifying it, or exposing people's mistakes in public
digital.help: If you are blackmailed or threatened, or your photos are posted without your permission, do not face it alone: report it to the platform, keep the evidence, contact the police or the cybercrime authority, and tell a trusted adult if you are young.

boundaries.label: Setting boundaries and saying “no”
boundaries.insight: Setting boundaries is not, in the Prophetic way, selfishness or harshness; it is part of giving every one who has a right their due: “Your Lord has a right over you, your soul has a right over you, and your family has a right over you; so give each one who has a right their due.” Allah Himself “does not charge a soul except [with that within] its capacity”, so you are not bound to carry more than you can for the sake of politeness. Privacy is sacred in the Quran: “and do not spy.” In the story of Barirah, when the Prophet ﷺ interceded for her to go back to her husband, he said: “I am only interceding,” and she said: “I have no need of him”; he made clear that she had the right to say no, even to his intercession. The Prophetic way joins firmness in the boundary with gentleness in the words: “Verily Allah is kind and He loves kindness,” and “speak to people good [words]”; a gentle, clear “no” is better than a “yes” that leaves you resentful and falling short.

now: Before agreeing to any request, say: “Let me think and get back to you”; the pause protects you from agreeing under pressure
Identify one boundary you need now (time, money, privacy, tone of speech) and phrase it in one short, polite sentence
Remember that a polite refusal does not cut family ties or spoil affection
week: Say “no” in one small situation, gently and clearly, without a long justification: “Sorry, I can't this time”
If the boundary is crossed again, talk to the person at a calm moment about its effect on you, not about their faults
Notice whose requests make you feel guilty whenever you refuse, and ask: is the guilt real, or a habit?
long: Keep your commitments in proportion to your energy and time; a little done steadily is better than a lot that stops
Learn to listen without taking on the responsibility of solving every problem
Respect other people's boundaries as you would like yours to be respected

questions: Which request do you always agree to and then regret? Why is it so hard to refuse?
Are you more afraid of the other person's displeasure than concerned with your own right, and your family's right, over you?
How can you say “no” in a way that keeps both affection and dignity?
avoid: Confusing boundaries with cutting ties; a boundary organises a relationship, it does not destroy it
Refusing harshly or sarcastically; firmness does not need to wound
Long apologies and over-justifying, until the boundary always seems open to negotiation
boundaries.help: If boundaries are crossed to the point of harm, harassment or ongoing control, this is no longer a matter of politeness: seek help from someone you trust or a specialised service.

self_worth.label: Self-worth
self_worth.insight: In the Quran and Sunnah a person's worth is not measured by looks, grades or likes: “Verily Allah does not look to your faces and your wealth, but He looks to your hearts and to your deeds,” and “the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you.” This frees you from chasing people's approval and puts you before a fair standard you are able to meet. The Prophetic way balances two things: confidence that drives you to strive, “The strong believer is better and more beloved to Allah than the weak believer, and there is good in both. Strive for what benefits you, seek help from Allah, and do not give up,” and humility that protects you from vanity, “So do not claim yourselves to be pure.” When the Prophet ﷺ was afraid at the first revelation, Khadijah told him: “Never! By Allah, Allah will never disgrace you”; a sincere, supportive word restores a soul's steadiness, and sometimes you need to say it to yourself.

now: Write down three things you did this week with sincerity and effort, not with an impressive result
When you hear “I am a failure” inside you, ask: would I say this to a friend in my position?
Pray: “O Allah, grant my soul its piety and purify it, for You are the best to purify it”
week: Choose one skill and practise it a little every day, accepting that you are a beginner
Reduce your exposure to what pushes you to despise yourself: accounts, comparisons, and people who criticise constantly
Ask someone who loves you and is honest with you to tell you the strengths they see in you
long: Build your worth on what lasts: your intention, your character and your effort, not on people's changing praise
Celebrate small progress; “the deeds most beloved to Allah are those done most consistently, even if they are few”
If harsh criticism from childhood still speaks inside you, understanding it with a specialist is a brave step, not a weakness

questions: Who set the standard you measure yourself by? Is it a fair standard?
What remains of you if grades, likes and positions disappear?
What, for you, is the difference between humility and despising yourself?
avoid: Tying your worth to your latest result, your looks, or one person's opinion
Waiting for perfection before starting; perfectionism is often fear in disguise
Despising yourself in the name of humility; humility means not looking down on people, not humiliating yourself
self_worth.help: If despising yourself becomes constant, or comes with isolation or thoughts of self-harm, consult a mental-health professional; seeking treatment is part of taking the means.
